idiom_name: opaque struct: incomplete type plus create/destroy functions
implementation_notes: The published header declares an incomplete type (typedef struct foo foo_t;) and functions that take foo_t *, while the struct definition and every accessor live in the .c file - clients can neither compute its size, name its fields nor depend on its layout, so changing the body recompiles only the library, never its users. This is the ancestor of handle/body in the language where the whole object is opaque: no pointer inside a visible object is needed, and the create/destroy pair replaces constructors and the destructor. Use it at any library or module boundary; inside a program that is always rebuilt as a whole it buys encapsulation but not the classic firewall, and it always costs a heap allocation plus a manual free.
pitfalls: An incomplete type cannot be allocated on the stack or embedded by value, so every instance costs an allocation, a null check and a manual free: forgetting foo_free leaks, calling it twice is undefined behaviour.
Nothing in the compiler enforces the lifecycle, so pair creation and destruction in one place (or wrap the handle in a small RAII struct from C++) instead of spreading frees across call sites.

A convenience _private.h header, a void * cast or struct-layout punning to reach the fields silently re-opens the firewall; keep the definition in exactly one translation unit and let the incomplete type do the enforcing.
